analysis.one_liner: Hands all fracking regulation, even on federal land, solely to the states.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have ended federal fracking rules on federal land, never got a committee vote and died when the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would give states the only power to write and enforce fracking rules, including for drilling on federal land such as national forests and Bureau of Land Management property. Today federal land is subject to federal standards set by agencies like the Bureau of Land Management; under this bill, state law alone would apply, with no federal minimum. It would also block any federal agency from issuing its own fracking rules or permit conditions.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies that drill on or under federal land. They would deal with one state rulebook instead of federal standards, and in states with lighter rules, would face fewer requirements for wells that produce oil and gas from public land.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil and gas drillers on federal land

how_it_helps.text: Gives states sole authority over fracking rules, removing any separate federal fracking regulation or permit requirement, including on federal land [S2][S3]
Requires fracking on federal land to follow only the law of the state where the land sits, replacing Bureau of Land Management oversight [S2][S3]
Does not change other federal environmental laws that cover related activity like wastewater disposal and air emissions, so companies would still follow those rules [S3]

analysis.who_pays: People who live near federal land drilling and drink water that could be affected, since there would be no federal fracking floor and states could set weaker or stronger rules as they chose. Taxpayers also bear risks from drilling on land the public owns.

drawbacks.text: With no federal floor, a state could set weaker fracking standards and those weaker rules would govern drilling on national forests and other public land in that state, since the bill makes state law the only rule even on federal land [S2][S3]

The bill cites older state and EPA studies from 2004-2014 finding no confirmed fracking groundwater contamination, but a rule written solely on those findings would bar newer federal agencies from applying updated evidence [S3]

A supporter would argue states already have detailed oil and gas rules and that other federal environmental statutes still cover related activity, so the change mainly removes duplicated permitting; an honest backer would still concede that federal land belongs to all Americans, not just the state it sits in

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a straightforward transfer of regulatory control from federal agencies to state governments. For drillers it cuts a layer of permitting. For the public the main cost is that fracking on federal land would be governed entirely by the state it sits in, so residents of other states who jointly own those lands would have no federal fracking standards protecting them, and neighboring states could not prevent weaker rules downstream or upwind. There is no federal minimum left in the bill.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Inhofe introduced the bill with seven Republican cosponsors on July 20, 2021 [S1][S4]
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Energy and Natural Resources Committee the same day; no hearing, markup, or vote ever followed [S5]
No Democrat sponsored or cosponsored the bill [S4]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas drillers are no better off, since nothing passed, but the bill's failure preserved federal fracking authority on federal land. The public lost nothing because the bill never advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal fracking oversight kept its authority

for.name: Sen. James Inhofe
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to give states sole fracking authority, including on federal land

for.name: 7 of 50 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill (Capito, Cruz, Cramer, Scott of South Carolina, Lummis, Lankford, and Inhofe's original group)

against.name: Sen. Joe Manchin
against.role: Chair, Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; it sat in committee until the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: All eight original sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans, no Democrat signed on, and the Democratic-chaired committee took no action on the bill.

industries.note: Drillers on federal land would no longer face a separate federal fracking rulebook; states alone would regulate, so in states with lighter rules their compliance costs fall. The savings come from the same oversight the public uses to protect water and air near public-land drilling.

industries.industry: Federal land management agencies (Bureau of Land Management)
industries.note: The bill strips these agencies of authority to write or enforce fracking rules or permit conditions on the land they manage, ending their role as the protector of federally owned mineral estates.
